e.t: This word means “indignation”—a strong feeling of displeasure or righteous anger directed toward something considered wrong. It names an emotional response rather than an action, teaching, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 7:11. Because the word appears in only one recorded occurrence and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the wider passage. Its central meaning remains a serious, stirred response against wrongdoing.

This word refers to the Adriatic Sea, a specific body of water named in the Greek New Testament. It functions as a geographic name rather than a description of a person, action, or quality. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 27:27. Its basic meaning is therefore straightforward: the Adriatic Sea. The surrounding passage is needed to explain what was happening there, but the name itself identifies the sea.

e.t: This Greek word means “be truthful” or “to be truthful.” It expresses the act of speaking or behaving in a truthful way rather than falsely. As a verb, it describes what someone does: living or communicating in keeping with what is true. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, appearing once in Galatians and once in Ephesians. Its precise emphasis in either verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage.

e.t: This word means “to help,” expressing the act of giving support or assistance to someone. In the Greek New Testament, it appears three times, each time describing help offered to others. Its basic sense is practical and relational: one person or group comes alongside another to provide needed support. The surrounding passage determines who receives the help and what form it takes, but the word itself centers on assisting rather than merely observing or acknowledging another person’s need.

e.t: This word means “to shut,” “to close,” or “shuts.” It describes the act of closing something so that access through it is stopped. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming an object or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 13:25. The exact force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the closing or shutting of an entrance or opening.

This Greek New Testament word can refer to a “bath” or a “bush,” so its exact sense must be determined by the sentence where it appears. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Luke 16:6. The word itself names a concrete thing rather than expressing an action or quality; however, the available verse text does not establish which of its two listed meanings is intended there.

This word refers to a bunch or cluster of grapes. It is a noun naming the fruit gathered together rather than a single grape. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Revelation 14:18. Its lexical meaning is “bunch of grapes” or “grape cluster.” The word itself identifies a grouped collection of grapes, while the surrounding passage determines its specific significance there.

This word means “tongue” or “tongues,” referring to the physical organ in the mouth. In New Testament usage, it can also name the speech associated with that organ, including tongues spoken by people. The word occurs 50 times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in 47 verses. Its central idea remains the tongue itself, with the surrounding passage determining whether attention is on the organ or its speech.

e.t: This word means “to serve”—to give help or carry out useful work for others. It is a verb describing active service rather than merely having a servant’s position. In the Greek New Testament, it is used for people serving Jesus, caring for others, and giving themselves in practical ministry. The word occurs 37 times in the Greek New Testament, showing that service is a recurring part of Christian life and conduct. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “Feast of Dedication,” naming a specific religious feast rather than describing a general act of dedicating something. It functions as the name of a festival and appears once in the Greek New Testament, in John 10:22. The word therefore points to the feast itself as a recognized occasion. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the name of this dedication feast.

This Greek New Testament word refers to “certainty” or “rebuke.” It can name something that gives firm confidence, or a corrective response that confronts wrong. The two glosses point to a settled assurance on one side and a forceful correction on the other; the surrounding wording determines which sense is active. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Hebrews 11:1.

This word describes someone who has been condemned to death, or condemned to die. It points to a death sentence or fate imposed on the person, rather than simply referring to death as an event. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in 1 Corinthians 4:9, so its broader uses cannot be established from repeated examples. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding words and passage.

This word describes something as “deserted,” presenting it as empty of the people or activity normally expected there. It can characterize a place or setting that has been left without its usual inhabitants. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 48 times, so it is used across a range of passages while retaining this central idea of being deserted. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what place or situation the surrounding text identifies.

This word means “easy,” describing something that does not present great difficulty. It can refer to an action, choice, or task viewed as more manageable than another possibility. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times, appearing in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Its precise force in a verse depends on what is being compared or discussed, but its central idea remains what is easy rather than difficult.

e.t: This word means “to sit down.” It describes the act of taking a seated position, whether someone settles down personally or is found sitting in a particular place. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times, so it refers to a straightforward physical action rather than expressing a broad abstract idea. The surrounding verse determines why the person sits and what significance that action has in the scene.

This word means “Zealot,” identifying a person known by that designation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times as a designation among Jesus’ disciples: once in Matthew and once in Mark. The word itself names the person; the surrounding passage is needed to understand any particular emphasis attached to him. Its consistent rendering as “Zealot” supports this straightforward meaning in both occurrences.

This word means “empty conceit” or “vain conceit”—an inflated view of oneself that has no real worth. It describes self-focused pride rather than a sound or valuable judgment. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Philippians 2:3, so its precise force there is understood from the surrounding instruction. The word itself points to conceit that is hollow, lacking genuine substance or value.

e.t: This verb means “to make unclean” or “to profane.” It describes treating something as unclean or making it unfit for what is considered holy or clean. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 14 times, including several occurrences in Matthew and Mark and one in Hebrews. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what person, thing, or practice is being described as unclean.

The word means “creature,” a broad term for a being or living thing. In its plural form, it refers to creatures generally rather than to one specific kind. This Greek New Testament word appears four times, in four verses, across 1 Timothy, James, and Revelation. Its central meaning remains general: an individual creature or creatures as a group, with the surrounding passage determining which beings are in view.

This word means “sickness,” referring to a condition of illness or poor health. It describes bodily affliction in a general sense rather than naming one particular disease. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Matthew, where it belongs to language describing sickness among people. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a state of sickness or illness.

This word means “certainly” or “surely,” expressing strong assurance that something is true or will happen. It functions as an emphatic word, strengthening a statement rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 6:14, and is rendered “Surely.” Its force is therefore one of confident confirmation: the speaker presents the statement as firmly established, not doubtful or merely possible.

This word refers to a myriad: an immense number or multitude. It describes quantity rather than a person, object, action, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times in seven verses, including passages that speak of very large gatherings or numbers. Its repeated use shows that it serves as a way to express an amount so great that the exact total is not the main focus.

This word means “like,” describing someone or something as similar to another rather than identical. It expresses likeness or shared resemblance and functions by connecting a person or thing with what it is compared to. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice: once in Acts 14:15 and once in James 5:17. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a comparison of likeness.

This word means “eye” or “eyes,” referring to the physical organ of sight. It can describe one eye or the eyes together, depending on the sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 100 times, showing that it is a common word for this visible part of the body. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word means “female servant” or “maidservant,” referring to a woman serving in a household or other setting. It is a noun describing the person’s role, not a personal name. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 13 times across 12 verses, including passages that refer to a servant woman. The surrounding passage determines the particular situation, but the central idea remains a woman serving under someone’s authority or responsibility.

This word means “what is made” or “workmanship”: something produced by a maker. It points to the result of making rather than to the act itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Romans 1:20 and Ephesians 2:10. Thus, it is a word about something made or produced. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the work or result brought forth by a maker.

This Greek New Testament word means “eagerness”—a ready, willing energy that moves someone toward action. It describes more than a passing interest: it points to a wholehearted readiness to do what is needed. In its five New Testament occurrences, it is especially associated with people’s willing response, active concern, or readiness to serve. The surrounding passage determines the particular action in view, but the central idea remains an eager willingness to act rather than reluctance or delay.

e.t: This word means “to fall” or “to fall down before” someone, and it can also describe something that “beats” against another thing. It may therefore express either a person falling before someone or an impact striking against something, depending on the sentence. The word occurs eight times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and Acts. Its central idea is forceful contact or a downward movement, whether caused by falling, bowing down, or something beating against another object.

This word means the “highest point” or “pinnacle” of a structure. It refers to the elevated top or summit of a building rather than to a person or an abstract idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Matthew 4:5 and Luke 4:9, and both passages use the word for the pinnacle of the temple. Thus, its ordinary sense is a physically high, prominent place. The surrounding passage determines what is happening there, but the word itself identifies the structure’s highest point.

This Greek New Testament word means distress or hardship—painful trouble that places a person under pressure. It describes difficult circumstances rather than a particular action or attitude. The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in Romans and 2 Corinthians. Its meaning can cover the experience of being burdened, afflicted, or severely troubled, while the surrounding passage determines the specific situation in view. It is therefore a broad word for serious distress and hardship endured in life.

e.t: This word means “to become like” or “to make like,” describing a movement toward likeness or conformity. As a verb, it can refer either to someone becoming like another or to one person making something like another. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Philippians 3:10. Its exact force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea is being shaped into likeness rather than merely observing or recognizing someone.

This word means a place or location—the particular space or position where someone or something is, goes, rests, or is found. It can refer to an ordinary physical location, such as a place to stay or gather, and can also describe a designated position or area. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 94 times, showing broad use for locations throughout the biblical narrative. Its exact force in a passage depends on what kind of place the surrounding sentence describes.

This word refers to a mother, especially a nursing mother who feeds and cares for her child. Its central idea is maternal care expressed through nourishing and tender provision. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Thessalonians 2:7. The specific force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, but its ordinary meaning points to a mother known for intimate, sustaining care.

This word means “later”. It points to a time that follows an earlier moment, action, or event. In ordinary speech, it helps arrange events in sequence by showing that something happens afterward rather than immediately. It appears twelve times in the Greek New Testament, so its basic function is consistent: it marks what comes after. The surrounding verse determines what event or time is being placed later, but the word itself simply directs attention forward in the sequence.

This word means “bronze” or “made of bronze.” It describes something consisting of, or associated with, the metal bronze. The basic sense is material and physical rather than an action or feeling. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated passages. Its precise force in Revelation 9:20 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself points plainly to bronze or something fashioned from bronze.

This word means a “relative,” referring to a person connected to someone through family ties. It is used as a noun to identify a family connection rather than an action, quality, or object. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Luke 1:36. Its precise reference in that verse must be understood from the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains a family relation.
